intro.html: Half of these words praise courage and half describe fear. Each one has its own shade: a valiant person fights hard, an intrepid one explores without trembling, a plucky one stands up even when small. On the fearful side, a timid person is shy, an apprehensive one worries about what is coming, and a craven one runs away in shame.
Two Latin roots help. timere means to fear: timid, timorous. trepidus means trembling, alarmed: trepidation is trembling fear, and intrepid (in- = not) means not trembling.
Watch the tone. Audacious can be praise (an audacious rescue) or blame (an audacious lie). The sentence tells you which.

words.def: brave and determined, especially in a hard fight
words.ex: The {valiant} firefighters carried every last puppy out of the burning shelter.
words.ctx: Though the little team was outnumbered and exhausted, it made a {valiant} stand in the final minutes and held the champions to a tie.
words.etym: From Old French vaillant, “stalwart, brave,” from valoir (to be worthy), from Latin valere, “to be strong.”

mn.cue: VAL the ANT: small but VALIANT
mn.text: Val the ant plants her feet and faces the hungry crow to guard her hill. Tiny Val is {valiant}.

scene.alt: A tiny ant stands bravely in front of a big crow to protect its anthill.

words.ex: The {intrepid} explorer paddled alone up the unmapped river.
words.ctx: Most of the divers turned back at the mouth of the dark sea cave, but the {intrepid} pair swam on, eager to see what lay inside.
words.etym: From Latin intrepidus, “unshaken, not alarmed”: in- (not) + trepidus (alarmed, trembling).
words.note: Intrepid has nothing to do with trips: it means not trembling.

mn.text: Trepid means trembling, and in- means not. Tia steps into the dark cave with her lantern without a single shiver: she is {intrepid}.

scene.alt: An explorer with a lantern walks calmly into a dark cave as a bat flutters past.

words.def: boldly daring, sometimes to the point of rudeness
words.ex: Asking the famous chef for her secret recipe on live TV was an {audacious} move.
words.ctx: The plan was {audacious}: the students would build a full-size rowboat in two weeks and sail it across the lake, though none of them had ever built anything bigger than a birdhouse.
words.etym: From Latin audax, “bold, daring,” from audere, “to dare.”
words.note: Audacious can be praise (an audacious rescue) or blame (an audacious lie); the context decides.

mn.cue: AWE-DACIOUS: so bold it leaves us in AWE
mn.text: Little Pip marches up to the king and asks to try on his crown. The whole court gasps in awe at such an {audacious} request.

scene.alt: A small boy points at the king’s crown and asks to try it on while the king looks shocked.

words.def: not discouraged by danger or difficulty
words.ex: The {dauntless} mail carrier delivered every letter through the blizzard.
words.ctx: After three failed launches, a weaker team might have quit, but the {dauntless} engineers fixed the valve, checked every bolt and tried again the next morning.
words.etym: Daunt comes from Old French danter, “to tame, subdue,” from Latin domitare (to tame); add -less, “without.”

mn.cue: DAWN-TLESS: out at DAWN in any storm
mn.text: Every day at dawn, through snow and howling wind, Greta delivers the mail. No storm can discourage her: she is {dauntless}.

scene.alt: A mail carrier marches through a snowstorm toward a mailbox with a letter.

words.def: brave and spirited, especially against the odds
words.ex: The {plucky} little goalie stopped shot after shot from the older team.
words.ctx: The puppy was the smallest in the litter, but it was {plucky}: it marched right up to the big farm dogs and demanded a share of the bone.

mn.text: The smallest duckling plucks up her courage and leaps into the pond first, ahead of all the big ducks. That brave little bird is {plucky}.

scene.alt: The smallest duckling leaps into the water first while two big ducks hang back nervously.

words.ex: The {timid} kitten hid under the bed whenever the doorbell rang.
words.ctx: At first Sofia was too {timid} to raise her hand, but by spring she was leading the class debate.
words.etym: From Latin timidus, “fearful,” from timere, “to fear.”

mn.text: When the friendly puppy trots up, little Tim hides behind his mom’s legs. Shy, easily frightened Tim is {timid}.

scene.alt: A toddler named Tim hides behind his mother as a friendly puppy says hello.

words.ex: The {timorous} deer froze at the snap of a twig.
words.ctx: Unlike his bold older sister, Leo was a {timorous} child who checked under the bed every night and never went near the creek alone.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin timorosus, “fearful,” from Latin timor (fear), from timere (to fear).

mn.cue: TIM-OR-MOUSE: a mouse full of fear
mn.text: Timmy the mouse trembles at every creak of the floor and every shadow on the wall. A creature that is always afraid is {timorous}.

scene.alt: A tiny mouse trembles with fear beside a piece of cheese.

words.def: worried that something bad may happen
words.ex: Jonah was {apprehensive} about his first day at the new school.
words.ctx: The sailors grew {apprehensive} as the sky darkened and the wind picked up, and the captain ordered everyone to tie down the sails before the storm hit.
words.etym: From Latin apprehendere, “to seize, grasp” (ad + prehendere); to apprehend a danger is to grasp in your mind that it may come.

mn.text: The hen spots a fox sniffing around the coop and cannot sleep all night, worrying about what he might do. She is {apprehensive}.

scene.alt: A worried hen watches a sneaky fox at the edge of the farm.

words.def: nervous fear about something that is about to happen
words.ex: With some {trepidation}, Kai stepped onto the stage for his first violin solo.
words.ctx: The villagers watched the rising river with {trepidation}, knowing that one more night of rain could flood every street in town.
words.etym: From Latin trepidatio, “alarm, trembling,” from trepidare, “to tremble.”

mn.text: Before his solo, Kai’s knees knock and his bow shakes. That trembling fear of what is about to happen is {trepidation}.

scene.alt: A boy with a violin trembles nervously on stage before his solo.

words.ex: The {craven} guard dropped his post and ran at the first sound of trouble.
words.ctx: Instead of admitting that he had broken the vase, the {craven} prince blamed a servant and hid in the tower until the fuss was over.

mn.text: When the cat creeps close, the raven flies off and leaves the little birds to fend for themselves. That shameful coward is a {craven} raven.

scene.alt: A raven flies off in a panic, leaving a small bird alone as a cat sneaks closer.

after.html: Craven is much harsher than timid. A timid person is shy and easily scared; a craven person abandons others to save himself. Calling someone craven is an insult.

items.q: In which sentence is audacious used as blame rather than praise?
choices: The audacious stranger cut to the front of the line and demanded to be served first.
The audacious rescue saved all twelve climbers.
Her audacious plan to cross the desert by bicycle succeeded.
The audacious young pilot set a new speed record.
items.why: Cutting the line and making demands is bold in a rude way; the other sentences admire the daring.

items.q: True or false: intrepid comes from the word trip, so it means “fond of travel.”
items.why: False. Intrepid comes from Latin in- (not) + trepidus (trembling): it means fearless. An intrepid person may travel, but the word is about courage.

items.q: The general called the officer craven because he…
choices: abandoned his soldiers to save himself
items.why: Craven means shamefully cowardly. Being careful, quiet or curious is not cowardice.

items.q: Which two words share the Latin root tim, “fear”?
items.why: Both timid and timorous come from Latin timere, “to fear.”
